analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable patient rights standards for HMOs and managed care plans, including emergency care, appeals, and the right to sue.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors in November 1999, the bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote as competing managed-care legislation moved instead.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a set of enforceable rights into federal law for people enrolled in HMOs and other managed care plans. It would guarantee coverage of emergency care without prior approval, direct access to OB-GYNs and specialists, continuity of treatment when a plan drops a doctor, external review when a plan denies care, an end to contract clauses restricting what doctors can tell patients, and a ban on paying doctors bonuses to limit care. It would also amend federal benefits law so patients could sue their health plan in state court for injury or wrongful death. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 100-plus million Americans in employer-sponsored and other managed care plans at the time: patients denied coverage for care their doctor deemed necessary, women seeking direct OB-GYN access, people needing emergency care at non-network hospitals, non-English speakers needing interpreters, and patients with ongoing specialist care. Enrollees would also gain the right to sue a health plan in state court for injury or death, which today is largely blocked by federal law for employer-based plans.

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees coverage of emergency care at any hospital, without prior approval, using a 'prudent layperson' standard, so patients no longer risk being billed for going to the ER.
Bars plans from limiting covered services that the treating professional deems medically necessary, and bans financial bonuses that pay doctors for skimping on care.

Requires plans to maintain adequate doctor networks (at least one primary care physician per 1,500 enrollees), offer a choice of at least three providers, cover out-of-network care, and give patients direct access to obstetricians and specialists.
Creates a right to appeal denied care, with an independent external review paid for by the plan, and forbids plans from punishing patients or doctors who appeal.
Lets patients sue their health plan in state court for personal injury or wrongful death, closing a loophole in federal benefits law that shielded HMOs from such lawsuits.

analysis.who_pays: Managed care plans and health insurers, through compliance costs, external-review expenses, and exposure to malpractice-style lawsuits; some of those costs would likely have been passed to employers and enrollees through premiums.

drawbacks.text: Requiring plans to cover out-of-network providers, pay for external reviews, and maintain minimum network ratios would raise administrative and medical costs, some portion of which would likely show up in higher premiums for employers and workers.

The bill would have overridden HMO cost-control tools — including a ban on paying doctors bonuses for limiting care and a bar on limiting drug access based on cost — which critics of patient-bill-of-rights legislation argued would drive up premiums and might cause some employers to drop coverage.

The generic substitution rule (allowed only when the generic has the same chemical composition, and substitution decided only by a physician) goes beyond standard pharmacy practice and could delay cheaper generic dispensing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections addressed real, well-documented harms of 1990s managed care and the bill preserved stronger state laws and allowed injury suits against plans, which backers considered essential to make the rights enforceable. The honest cost is that external review of every denial, guaranteed out-of-network coverage, and expanded liability would raise insurers' operating costs, some of which would likely pass into premiums for employers and workers; the stricter generic-substitution rule could also raise drug costs slightly. The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote, so its costs were never weighed publicly against its benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, was never taken up, and died when the Congress ended, while broader patient-protection bills dominated the debate.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on November 8, 1999, late in the first session of the 106th Congress.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the Commerce and Education and Workforce committees, and on November 17, 1999, to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the House, and the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001.
Its core provisions overlapped with the larger patients'-bill-of-rights debate of that era, including the right to sue health plans, which Congress ultimately did not enact in that session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs, which avoided federal patient-rights mandates and continued to be shielded from malpractice suits by federal benefits law.

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.role: Health Insurance Association of America and allied employer coalitions
against.what_they_did: Opposed patient-protection legislation including expansion of plan liability during the 1999-2000 managed care debate.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Chose to move narrower, competing managed-care proposals rather than comprehensive patient-rights bills with a right to sue; no hearing was ever held on this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote, so no partisan split on it was ever recorded. Broader patients'-bill-of-rights bills of the era split largely on party lines, with Republicans favoring limited lawsuit rights and Democrats backing broader ones.

industries.industry: Managed care plans and health insurers
industries.note: The bill would impose federal standards on networks, referrals, emergency coverage, appeals, and prescription drug coverage, and would let enrollees sue plans for injury or death, ending their broad legal immunity under federal benefits law.
Mostly a cost: plans would face compliance costs and liability exposure that would partly pass through to employers, though workers in their plans would gain appeal and liability rights.
Doctors gain authority over medical decisions, a ban on financial incentives to limit care, an end to contract 'gag clauses', and continuous referrals for ongoing specialty care.
